**How much difference could a vaccination campaign make?** Most models are built to answer questions like this: how many infections would an intervention prevent, and more than another use of the same effort? This tutorial compares a one-off campaign, vaccination over the year, and a response that cuts transmission, as scenarios. It then adds the school calendar, and runs the scenarios many times to see how sure the answer is.

By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- give a vaccine to a chosen group of people, once or over time;
- change a parameter of the model from a given date, for interventions that don't hand anything out, or for a calendar such as school terms;
- compare several scenarios by name, and read the difference between them from a table;
- run each scenario many times, and tell the uncertainty in an outcome from the uncertainty in a difference.

## The model so far

This is the model from [T4 – Age groups and contacts](t4_ages.qmd): an SEIR model of 100,000 people in three age groups, mixing by a contact matrix. Most people are immune, but only 80% of children, and 10 people are infectious on 1 January 2025. Each case at the start infects about 2.5 others:

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5]) # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day

infection   = S >> E @ beta*I       # Infection, at a rate of β times the contacts with infectious people
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),                           # 10 people infectious at the start
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the share of people in each

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
settings = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')

sim = ss.Sim(measles, **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```

With R0 = 16, preventing an outbreak needs more than 1 − 1/16 ≈ 94% of people immune. Here about 89% are, so about 8,800 people are infected, mostly children.

## A vaccination campaign

A vaccine has two parts in a model: the **product**, what it does to those who get it (here, it cuts their chance of infection by 93%, about what one dose of measles vaccine does), and the **delivery**, who gets it and when. [`ss.vaccinate()`](../api/interventions.qmd) takes both: the efficacy, the group (`who=`), the share reached (`coverage=`), and when (`when=`).

Suppose a campaign on 1 March, two months into the outbreak, reaches 80% of children under 15. A scenario is a sim with its own interventions; make one for each, labeled, and run them together with `ss.parallel()`:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
campaign = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, who=measles.age < 15, when='2025-03-01', coverage=0.8)

msim = ss.parallel({
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(measles, **settings),
    'Campaign':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, **settings),
})
msim.plot('measles.infection')
```

## R

```r
# With measles and age_contacts as in T4; a function makes each scenario's sim, with these settings
make_sim <- function(...) {
  Sim(measles, networks = age_contacts, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2026-01-01", ...)
}
campaign <- vaccinate(efficacy = 0.93, who = measles$age < 15, when = "2025-03-01", coverage = 0.8)

msim <- parallel(list(
  "No intervention" = make_sim(),
  "Campaign"        = make_sim(interventions = campaign)
))
msim$plot("measles.infection")
```

## Explicit

```{python}
vaccine = ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.93, leaky=True) # The product: everyone vaccinated is 93% less likely to be infected
campaign_explicit = ss.vaccinate(vaccine, who=measles.age < 15, when='2025-03-01', coverage=0.8, name='campaign') # The delivery: who, when, and how many
settings_explicit = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01', dt=ss.days(1), unit='day', solver='ode', aging=False)

msim_explicit = ss.parallel({
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(diseases=measles, **settings_explicit),
    'Campaign':        ss.Sim(diseases=measles, interventions=campaign_explicit, **settings_explicit),
})
msim_explicit.plot('measles.infection')
```
:::

The scenarios are the same until 1 March (each is a separate run). After the campaign, the outbreak peaks within weeks, since those already infected still fall ill, then dies away, cut from about 8,800 infections to 2,200.

Like real campaigns, it reaches children whether or not they are immune, so most doses go to children already protected; what matters is the share of *susceptible* children reached. Vaccination doesn't cure anyone already infected. Each delivery has its own results, such as doses delivered:

```{python}
print('Doses delivered:', round(msim.sims['Campaign'].results.campaign.delivered.sum()))
```

This vaccine protects everyone vaccinated by 93% (it is "leaky"). Measles vaccine is closer to all or nothing, fully protecting 93% and the rest not at all (`leaky=False`); over one outbreak, the two give nearly the same result. Vaccines can also wane, need several doses, or protect against transmission rather than infection; see [Products](../user_guide/interventions_products.qmd).

## Vaccination over time, and changing a parameter

Without `when=`, a delivery reaches people over time: each person once, on becoming eligible, or, with a rate as the coverage, at that rate while eligible. Here, children under 15 are reached at a rate that would vaccinate 80% of them in a year. `ss.probperyear(0.8)` is a probability of 0.8 over a year, which Starsim converts to a probability per day:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
gradual = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, who=measles.age < 15, coverage=ss.probperyear(0.8))
```

## R

```r
gradual <- vaccinate(efficacy = 0.93, who = measles$age < 15, coverage = ss$probperyear(0.8))
```

## Explicit

```{python}
p_day = 1 - (1 - 0.8)**(1/365) # The daily probability that gives 0.8 over 365 days
gradual = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.93, who=measles.age < 15, coverage=ss.probperday(p_day))
```
:::

This is not routine childhood immunization, which vaccinates each child at an age (`who=ss.at_age(ss.months(9))`) and matters over many years, with births (see [Interventions](../user_guide/interventions_interventions.qmd#rounds-and-routine-delivery)).

Some interventions change how the disease spreads rather than giving people anything: isolating cases, tracing contacts, or keeping unvaccinated children home. These are changes to a parameter. [`ss.modify()`](../api/connectors.qmd) changes one from a date (and, with `stop=`, until another), without overwriting it, so when it stops, the parameter has its own value again. Here, a response from 1 March cuts transmission by 30%. Written out, `start=` is a function of the sim's date:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
response = ss.modify(measles.pars.beta, multiply=0.7, start='2025-03-01')
```

## R

```r
response <- modify(measles$pars$beta, multiply = 0.7, start = "2025-03-01")
```

## Explicit

```{python}
def response_factor(sim):
    """ 0.7 from 1 March, and 1 (no change) before """
    return 0.7 if sim.now >= ss.date('2025-03-01') else 1.0

response = ss.modify(measles.pars.beta, multiply=response_factor)
```
:::

A time series changes it at several dates, each value holding until the next: `ss.modify(measles.pars.beta, multiply=ss.timeseries({'2025-03-01': 0.7, '2025-06-01': 0.9}), start='2025-03-01')` cuts transmission by 30% from March and by 10% from June. [Interventions](../user_guide/interventions_interventions.qmd) covers other options, such as changes only for some people, or only while cases are high.

## Comparing scenarios

`ss.parallel()` runs the four scenarios at once on the computer's cores:

```{python}
sims = {
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(measles, **settings),
    'Campaign':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, **settings),
    'Over the year':   ss.Sim(measles, interventions=gradual, **settings),
    'Response':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=response, **settings),
}
msim = ss.parallel(sims)
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

Vaccinating over the year helps less than the campaign, since most children are reached after the peak. The response slows the outbreak, but it goes on, since nobody is made immune.

[`msim.summarize()`](../api/run.qmd) gives each result over the run for each scenario: the total of a flow, such as infections, and the final value of a state. `.loc[...]` picks one result:

```{python}
summary = msim.summarize()
summary.loc['measles_infection']
```

The campaign prevents the most infections but needs the most doses at once; the response prevents fewer but needs no vaccine. A model can't make that choice, but can say what each option buys. Compare peaks and timing as well as totals, and run long enough: an intervention can delay infections past the end of the run, so a lower total over a short run is not the same as infections prevented.

## School terms

Before vaccination, measles epidemics in England and Wales followed the school calendar: transmission among children rose when schools opened and fell in the holidays. To model this, split the contacts into school and the rest: suppose 6 of children's 10 daily contacts with other children are at school. Each set is its own named `ss.contacts()`, adding up to the same matrix as before. [`ss.timeseries()`](../api/internals.parameters.qmd) gives a value from each of a set of dates until the next: here, 1 in term and 0 in the holidays (simplified), repeating every year (`period=ss.years(1)`). `ss.modify()` multiplies the school contacts by it. Written out, the calendar is a plain function of the sim's date:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
school = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[6, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]], name='school')
other  = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[4, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]], name='other')
terms = ss.timeseries({
    '2025-01-01': 0, # New Year holidays
    '2025-01-06': 1, # Spring term
    '2025-04-07': 0, # Spring holidays
    '2025-04-21': 1, # Summer term
    '2025-07-21': 0, # Summer holidays
    '2025-09-01': 1, # Autumn term
    '2025-12-19': 0, # Winter holidays
}, period=ss.years(1))
holidays = ss.modify(school, multiply=terms)
```

## R

```r
school <- contacts(ages = c(0, 15, 65), matrix = rbind(c(6, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 0)), name = "school")
other  <- contacts(ages = c(0, 15, 65), matrix = rbind(c(4, 6, 1), c(3, 8, 1), c(3, 6, 3)), name = "other")
terms <- ss$timeseries(list(
  "2025-01-01" = 0, # New Year holidays
  "2025-01-06" = 1, # Spring term
  "2025-04-07" = 0, # Spring holidays
  "2025-04-21" = 1, # Summer term
  "2025-07-21" = 0, # Summer holidays
  "2025-09-01" = 1, # Autumn term
  "2025-12-19" = 0  # Winter holidays
), period = years(1))
holidays <- modify(school, multiply = terms)
```

## Explicit

```{python}
school = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[6, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]], name='school')
other  = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[4, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]], name='other')

def terms(sim):
    """ 1 in term and 0 in the holidays, the same every year """
    day = (sim.now.month, sim.now.day)
    in_term = (1, 6) <= day < (4, 7) or (4, 21) <= day < (7, 21) or (9, 1) <= day < (12, 19)
    return 1.0 if in_term else 0.0

holidays = ss.modify(school, multiply=terms)
```
:::

The holidays are part of how the town works, not a policy, so they go in `connectors=` rather than `interventions=`, though they work the same way. Suppose measles arrives on 1 May instead, and compare with and without the holidays:

```{python}
calendar = dict(networks=[school, other], total_pop=100_000, start='2025-05-01', stop='2026-05-01')
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No school holidays': ss.Sim(measles, **calendar),
    'School holidays':    ss.Sim(measles, connectors=holidays, **calendar),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

The summer holidays come as the outbreak grows fastest. They flatten it rather than stop it: the peak is about half as high, and the outbreak lasts into the winter, rising again when schools reopen. The total infected hardly changes, since it is set by the town's immunity, but the load on clinics at any one time is much lower. Over many years, a calendar like this sets the timing of epidemics.

A smooth yearly cycle is another way to give transmission a season: `ss.seasonal(mean=0.14, amplitude=0.2, peak='January')`, in place of β, varies 20% either side of 0.14. A time series can also hold a rate, a duration, or a coverage, and be read from a file. See [Time](../user_guide/building_time.qmd) and [Parameters](../user_guide/building_parameters.qmd).

## Many runs

So far each scenario has run once, as an ODE: the expected course of the outbreak. But two identical towns don't have the same outbreak, since who meets whom differs by chance, and this matters most when cases are few. Is the campaign's effect as certain as one run suggests?

A stochastic model draws at random the number of people who move between states each day. With `solver='binomial'` (a chain-binomial model), it is the same model, solved differently. `n_runs=30` runs each scenario 30 times, each with its own random numbers:

```{python}
msim = ss.parallel({
    'No intervention': ss.Sim(measles, solver='binomial', **settings),
    'Campaign':        ss.Sim(measles, interventions=campaign, solver='binomial', **settings),
}, n_runs=30)
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

The plot shows the median of the runs and the band holding 95% of them (`lines=True` shows every run). Without the campaign, the outbreaks differ mainly in timing; with it, in size too, since the further an outbreak has grown by 1 March, the less the campaign can prevent. As the runs peak on different days, the median curve is lower and broader than any one outbreak.

To count a scenario's infections, total each run, then summarize the totals. `msim.summarize()` does this for every result: the median, the range holding 95% of runs (`low` and `high`), the mean, and the standard deviation:

```{python}
msim.summarize().loc['measles_infection']
```

Run 1 of each scenario uses the same random numbers, as does run 2, and so on. So until 1 March each pair of runs is the same outbreak, and the difference afterwards is the effect of the campaign, not chance. `summarize(baseline=...)` gives these differences, run by run (negative here means infections averted):

```{python}
msim.summarize(baseline='No intervention').loc['measles_infection']
```

The campaign averts about 5,500 to 7,500 infections in 95% of pairs, 6,700 in the median. This is only the uncertainty from chance: every run has the same β, immunity, and contacts. Uncertainty in those, often larger, comes from varying them too, as in [T7 – Data and calibration](t7_calibration.qmd).

A run's random numbers come from its seed, `rand_seed` (by default 1); `n_runs=30` uses seeds 1 to 30. The same model and seed give the same result every time, on any computer, so an odd run can be looked at again. Keep the seed fixed while checking a change to a model, and use many seeds before drawing a conclusion. See [Scenarios](../user_guide/running_scenarios.qmd) and [Random numbers](../user_guide/mechanics_random.qmd).

## Exercises

1. The campaign above is run on 1 March. How many infections does it prevent if it is run on 1 February instead, or on 1 May? What does this say about how quickly a campaign should follow the first cases?
2. Add a scenario that combines the campaign and the response (`interventions=[campaign, response]`). Is its effect the sum of the two on their own? Why not?
3. Start the outbreak with 2 infectious people rather than 10 (`init_n=dict(I=2)`), and run the model with no intervention 50 times as a stochastic model. In what share of runs does the outbreak die out? Compare this with (1/R)², where R ≈ 2.5 is the reproduction number at the start: roughly the chance that the chains of infection started by both people die out.

- [Covasim: Using interventions](https://docs.covasim.org/tutorials/tut_interventions.html): interventions, including changes to contacts by setting, in an agent-based model of COVID-19
- [Covasim: Running scenarios](https://docs.covasim.org/tutorials/tut_running.html): running scenarios many times and plotting their uncertainty
- [epydemix: Modeling interventions](https://epydemix.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/03_Modeling_Interventions.html): interventions on contact layers, such as school closures, in a compartmental model
